1:
Four of them open by objecting to the chapter division. Calvin says it shows how absurdly chapters are divided, the sentence being cut off from what it belongs to and joined to what it has no connection with; Clarke says it is out of all proper place; Barnes says it was improperly separated; Robertson says it belongs to the preceding chapter. Henry alone declines to decide, noting only that the dividers made it a preface while it seems a better close. Chrysostom, having no chapter numbers to quarrel with, marks the same seam from inside: Paul, having finished the discourse on idol-sacrifices, passes to a lesser complaint, it being his manner not to set down all the heavy accusations together.

On being followed at all, the warnings outnumber the encouragements. Calvin draws two rules, that Paul prescribes nothing he had not practised and directs everyone to Christ as the only pattern, then warns against misdirected imitation: men strive after the manner of apes to copy whatever persons of great influence do, and many evils have entered the Church through this desire to imitate all the actions of the saints. Henry sets the limit in an image, that Christ's pattern is a copy without a blot and no man's else is, so apostles should be left when they deviate from their Master. Gill makes it concrete, that Paul sought God's glory and not popular applause.

The praise is read as tactical by all and ironical by none. Ellicott says the coming rebuke is, courteously introduced with commendation, suggests the Corinthians had boasted of their obedience in the letter Paul answers, and notes the two words are unequal: he exhorts them to be imitators but praises them only for bearing him in mind. Calvin meets the harder objection, that Paul had just blamed them for much, by answering that individuals were infected with one vice or another while the form he prescribed was kept by the body.

The word traditions then splits the two ends of the catena. Calvin turns it at once into controversy, the Papists arming themselves with this passage; he concedes that certain apostolic traditions were never written down, but denies they were doctrine or necessary to salvation, holding that they concerned order and government, every church being free to frame a form suitable to itself. Robertson handles the same word without polemic: it means merely something handed on, bad as in the Gospels or wholly good as here; and he enlarges it into a remark that there is a constant conflict between new and old in science, medicine, law and theology, the obscurantist rejecting all the new and holding to the old both true and untrue.

The chain of headship is expounded carefully at both ends. Ellicott insists the allusion is not to Christ as head of the human race but as head of the Body, so the equality taught in Galatians is one of order and not of disorder, each member being not an isolated irresponsible atom but part of an organic whole. Calvin meets the same tension by dividing the spheres: there Paul treats the spiritual kingdom, where external qualities are not regarded, here outward propriety, which belongs to ecclesiastical polity. On the last clause Calvin says it is spoken of Christ as mediator, inferior as having assumed our nature and otherwise of one essence with the Father; Wesley argues from the parallel, that a difference of divine nature can no more be inferred here than a difference of human nature between man and woman. Robertson adds that since the noun is anarthrous and predicate the sense is rather, God is the head of Christ. Clarke closes with a dry sentence the rest of the chapter will test, that so far there is no difficulty here; and Lightfoot opens his rabbinic annotation with the rule that wise men are not to pray uncovered.
4:
What praying and prophesying covers is settled first, and widened as it goes. Clarke takes prophesying from Paul's own definition, speaking to men for edification, exhortation and comfort, which comprehends all we mean by preaching. Wesley narrows it to speaking by the immediate power of God. Gill goes widest, applying it not to whoever leads but to every worshipper who joins in the prayer and hears the word, and adding that prophesying may even mean the singing of psalms, since the Targum renders the prophesying of Saul's company as singing praise.

The custom Paul lays down runs against the one he was raised in, and two of them say so. Ellicott observes that among the Jews the man prayed with head covered and face veiled in the Tallith, confessing his unworthiness to speak face to face with God, so the ruling shows how completely Paul had overcome his old prejudice; and he credits him with a profound insight, that an external symbol will infallibly modify doctrine, so keeping this one might have hindered the recognition of every soul's direct communion with the Father. Clarke says the same without the psychology, that the decision was in point blank hostility to the canons of the Jews, and sends his reader to Lightfoot, whose note stands in the same catena. Robertson supplies the Greek side, that men and women alike prayed bareheaded.

Whether women might prophesy at all is the question underneath, and the answers run the whole distance. Clarke is boldest: the words mean precisely the same for the woman as for the man, so some women as well as some men might speak to edification; the gift was foretold by Joel and claimed by Peter, without which the prophecy could not have been fulfilled. Ellicott resolves the tension with the commands of silence by the size of the gathering, those meaning the whole Church and these smaller meetings; and he rejects the alternative that Paul argues only for argument's sake, asking whether he would have laboured a merely forensic discussion of conditions for functions he was about to forbid outright. Calvin takes that rejected reading, holding that in condemning the manner Paul does not commend the act but defers his censure to the fourteenth chapter. Barnes agrees and adds a rule: the prophetesses were inspired, so their example is no warrant now unless the same evidence appears. Wesley allows it only under an immediate impulse of the Spirit, and Robertson says Paul condemns not the act but the breach of custom.

What the bare head signalled in Corinth is documented at length. Robertson reports that only the courtesans, so numerous in that city, went unveiled, and that slave-women wore the shaven head, which was also the adulteress's punishment; his conclusion is that Paul is not telling Christian women to put themselves on a level with courtesans. Clarke gathers the same from further afield, Tacitus on the German husband who cut off his wife's hair and turned her out before her relatives, and Euripides on Helen, who cut off only the very points of her hair to preserve her beauty. Ellicott turns it into a reductio: let the woman who insists on speaking uncovered carry the principle out and claim the right to crop her hair, and see what would be thought of her; it is illogical to urge a general principle as universal when you yourselves admit exceptions. Lightfoot raises the obvious objection, that she might wear her hair loose, nature having given it for a covering, and asks whether the apostle will suffer that. Calvin guesses at the motive, that women with beautiful hair uncovered to show it off; and he keeps the matter proportionate, saying it were no crime for a teacher to wear a cap in the pulpit, provided he uncovers in view of the Church, even if he puts it on again for fear of catching cold.
7:
The ground of the argument shifts, as Ellicott points out, from the woman's relation to man and the man's to Christ, to the same pair in the physical creation: man the image and glory of God, woman the glory of the man. Ellicott adds that the spiritual equality of husband and wife does not upset this, and that destroying its outward expression would soon obliterate the fact; and he restricts the passage to married women, thinking it unlikely any unmarried woman had attempted such an outrage. Calvin denies the restriction: some limit the teaching to wives because virgins are not under a husband's authority, but this is a mistake, since Paul looks beyond it to God's eternal law, and the appeal to what is seemly would otherwise fail, it being no more becoming for a virgin to be shaven. Barnes reads the covering as the emblem of her station, and Gill narrows the ruling another way, that a man is not forbidden to cover his head at any time, but only in public worship.

The word rendered power then divides them, both sides arguing from usage. Ellicott and Lightfoot insist it everywhere means a power one holds oneself and never a power held over one; Lightfoot says so of a thousand places, and Ellicott calls it the fatal objection to the received view. Ellicott then identifies the power with the woman's long hair, called her glory a few verses later, noting that Callistratus twice uses the word of an abundance of hair; and he finds it eminently Pauline to call the badge of subordination a power. Against them Calvin, Clarke and Robertson take the word as metonymy for the token of another's authority, Calvin saying she is subject and should wear a token of subjection, Clarke citing Theophylact and Photius for the veil as the symbol of being under power.

The angels divide them five ways. Wesley says only that they attend, and nothing indecent should be done before them. Robertson agrees, adding that the angels themselves veil their faces before Jehovah, and dismissing the alternatives that they are preachers or evil angels who could be tempted. Clarke, following Pearce, takes them for holy angels present in worship on the Jewish notion, which he supports from Josephus. Calvin knows and rejects as too forced the proposal that ministers are meant, Malachi having called priests angels. Lightfoot goes the other way: if the power is a veil, then by angels he understands devils, so called in this same epistle. Ellicott offers the boldest reading, that Paul's mind runs on from the first chapters of Genesis to the sixth, where the sons of God are angels in the Greek, and that he uses the story of their fall as an argument with those who believed it, without endorsing it; against Meyer he keeps them good angels, since the point is that they should not be tempted.

How hard the verse is, all concede. Ellicott calls its two clauses perhaps the most difficult passages in the New Testament; Clarke says few portions of Scripture have given rise to such variety of conjecture, that our translators were so puzzled they inserted one of the largest marginal readings anywhere in their work, and that Locke ingenuously acknowledged he did not understand the words. Clarke then lays out the apparatus: Toup of Cornwall's emendation making it when she goes out, rejected because no manuscript or version supports it; and an early printed Vulgate reading simply that the woman ought to have a covering upon her head, and because of the angels, matched by his own old manuscript English, that she schal haue a veyl on her heuyd, and for aungels. Ellicott sets aside the same conjectures on principle, since altering a difficult word would naturally simplify it, whereas these make it harder. Clarke ends by handing the question to the reader.
11:
A corrective follows at once, and the voices treat it as deliberate. Ellicott says these are words of caution lest the declaration of subordination be exaggerated or perverted, since subordination implies mutual connection and not isolation; and he sets two facts side by side, that the first woman was made out of man and that every man since has been born of a woman, the Greek marking the first as a finite act and the second as a continued process. Calvin and Gill take the clause in the Lord as the limit, this mutual dependence holding within the Christian order. Barnes reads the whole as designed to keep the woman from being depressed by what precedes,; and Ellicott adds that Paul traces all up to God.

The appeal is then handed back to the readers, and what nature means is disputed. Ellicott offers two senses, the inborn feeling of what is seemly as against revelation, or the arrangement of things in creation, and prefers the first, comparing the heathen who without revelation do by nature the things of the law. Robertson takes both, a native sense of propriety in addition to custom but resting on the objective difference in the constitution of things. Clarke argues it as biology, that the male's hair rarely grows like the female's unless art is used, so that long hair is truly womanish.

Clarke spends his longest note on hair. The Greeks of the province in which Corinth stood were noted for theirs, so that Homer calls them the long-haired Achaeans; but long hair was not in repute among the Jews, and the Nazarites who let it grow did so as a token of humiliation, which Clarke thinks Paul may have had in view, so that it stands condemned as both humiliating and womanish. He then turns on his own century, guessing that Paul may mean the dressed and frizzled hair that shallow and effeminate men affect, and declaring there is perhaps no sight more ridiculous than a high-dressed, curled and powdered head, over which the operator takes considerable pains and the silly patient loses much time and comfort. Robertson answers from the ground, citing a papyrus in which a priest is accused of letting his hair grow long, and Vincent on the catacomb sculptures, where the women have a close-fitting head-dress and the men short hair. Lightfoot adds a rabbinic story of the daughter of Nicodemus reduced to poverty; Wesley keeps to the plain sense, that nature has taught the woman what to wear.

The last verse is read two ways and then made to carry a great deal. Ellicott reports the suggestion that the custom disowned is the contentiousness rather than the uncovering, and prefers the latter, the Apostle's object being to show how such an objector must be met. Clarke takes it as covering both faults, the woman's bare head and the man's long hair, sanctioned by no church of God whether among Jews or Gentiles. Robertson notes that the word for contentious occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and wonders drily whether the disputatious brother existed only here. Ellicott makes the appeal itself the point, that it is to the churches in the plural and not the Church, so what is quoted is not authority but uniformity of practice, and Corinth has no right to be exceptional. He then draws two morals: that as with slavery, Christianity did not efface recognised social arrangements by sudden revolution but leavened the world gradually, coming not to unsex woman but to abolish her real wrongs without yielding to a clamour for imaginary rights; and that the temporary application of the rule has been universally kept while the eternal principle behind it has been forgotten, which is why the apostolic writers were withheld from laying down minute directions for worship, men being apt in servile obedience to rules to forget the principles beneath them.
17:
How the abuse arose is reconstructed twice, differently. Chrysostom, nearest in time, describes an institution decaying: as the first three thousand had all things common, so an outflowing of that communion descended to later believers, who, being some rich and some poor, did not lay all their goods in the middle but opened their tables on stated days, so that after the communion of the Mysteries all went to a common table, the rich bringing provisions and inviting the destitute. Afterward the custom became corrupt, the reason being the party spirit that made men say I am of this teacher and I of that; Paul had attacked it by putting his own name at the head of the list, since if it were wickedness in his case it was much more so in lesser men. Clarke reconstructs it as doctrinal corruption: false teachers in the apostle's absence had them keep the Supper as the Jews kept the passover, a regular meal with bread solemnly broken and a cup of blessing, so that the divine institution became part of an ordinary meal, with something referring to our Lord's institution appended at the end.

Two of them notice that the first of all has no second. Robertson observes that no antithesis is expressed, and that this is the only reason Paul gives. Ellicott concludes that the first point is the disorder at the Supper and the second the abuse of spiritual gifts in the next chapter, two branches of one subject; and he draws a caution from it, that this is not a treatise but a letter answering a letter, so that if we had the epistle it replies to, much that puzzles us would be as clear as it was to those who first received it.

The half-belief draws the warmest note here. Ellicott calls the words full of the courtesy characteristic of the Apostle, and turns them on the reader: the general practice is to believe more than we are told, whereas St. Paul believed only a part. Robertson accounts for the report differently, that the rumours were so constant the apostle keeps on hearing them. Clarke names the parties and puts them in the room, the followers of Paul, of Cephas and of Apollos eating separately in the same house; Gill and Henry take the divisions as the old factions of the first chapter carried into the assembly.

What separates divisions from heresies is worked at from three sides. Calvin reports the ancient usage, that heresy lay in disagreement as to doctrine and schism in alienation of affection, and grants that heresy is the root of schism, but takes the words here as less and greater: schisms are secret grudges, where every one is mightily pleased with his own way and finds fault with all that others do, while heresies are open hostility with men deliberately dividing into parties. Robertson compresses the same into an epigram, that heresy is theoretical schism and schism practical heresy. Ellicott insists neither word can mean bodies separated from the Church, only parties within it, and adds that Christ himself may have used this very word, since Justin Martyr attributes it to him, so that Paul may be quoting an unrecorded saying. Calvin finds a lovely consolation in the purpose of it: so far should we be from being cast down at seeing the Church torn, that even if sects start up on every side we ought to stand firm, since this is how hypocrites are detected and the sincerity of believers tried as gold in the furnace; but he refuses the labyrinth of a fatal necessity, which comes not from fate but from the reprobates whom Satan governs. Robertson brings Findlay's image of such parties as a magnet for unsound and unsettled minds. Barnes and Wesley keep to the plainer sense, that God permits the divisions that the approved may be made manifest.
20:
What Paul denies is stated carefully. Calvin says it is not that a single abuse set aside the institution of Christ and reduced it to nothing, but that they polluted the sacrament by observing it wrongly, since we say in common speech that a thing is not done at all if it is not done aright; he notes that others read the words as meaning it is not lawful to eat, and thinks the sense comes to much the same. Ellicott renders it that when they assemble in the same place it is not to eat the supper dedicated to the Lord, and observes that the phrase used here is more general than the one Paul uses further down, the whole meal being dedicated by its union with the sacramental Supper. Robertson notes that the adjective is not a merely biblical word, being found in inscriptions and papyri in the sense of imperial, as of the imperial treasury, and that it may cover both the love-feast and the Eucharist; his verdict on the proceedings is that they made a mere grab-game of it.

Where the custom came from is Calvin's question, and he answers it historically. He reports an earlier opinion that it began with the love-feasts, the rich at first bringing provisions to feast with the poor indiscriminately and afterwards excluding them to guzzle over their delicacies alone; he adds that the Latin apologists show the custom to be very ancient, and that Pliny appears to describe it in his letter to Trajan, where the Christians of Bithynia said it was their habit to depart and come together again to take an innocent repast in common. Calvin's own guess is that it arose from the sacrificial feasts of Jews and Gentiles alike, Christians correcting the faults of those rites while retaining some resemblance, so that the poor were entertained at the expense of the rich and the table was open to all. Lightfoot disputes the whole identification, wondering that the love-feasts named in Jude should be expounded from this passage, and citing Beza and Baronius as those who join the two. Clarke keeps to the plain picture, that each brought his own provisions and made as ample a supper as he could before what was called the Lord's Supper.

The speed of the corruption then draws Calvin's sharpest remark. It is truly wonderful, and next to a miracle, that Satan could have accomplished so much in so short a time, and it warns us how much a long continued custom can effect while unsanctioned by a single declaration of the word of God: Paul was at hand to interfere here, but what must the state of matters have been after the death of the Apostles? Yet this, he says, is the great strength of the Papists, that a thing is ancient and was done long ago, and should therefore carry the weight of a revelation from heaven. On the conduct itself Robertson quotes the summary that hungry poor were meeting intoxicated rich at what was supposed to be a supper of the Lord, and observes that Paul's closing question is a deliberative subjunctive expressing his bewilderment. Ellicott finds the shame doubled, arising both from the contrast between poverty and wealth brought into direct contact and from the evident dislike of the rich to eat with the poor. Clarke and Barnes agree that those who have not are not merely the unprovisioned but the poor, unable to furnish themselves as others did; Wesley and Gill add that they should have taken their ordinary meal at home and come together only for the sacrament.
23:
Whether Paul means a direct revelation is settled by grammar. Ellicott argues that he does: the emphatic I, the singular verb, and above all the phrase from the Lord, since the other apostles had their knowledge not from the Lord but from their own eyes and ears; how Christ communicated it we are not told, and the method raised no difficulty for those who first heard. Robertson agrees in a line, calling it a direct claim to revelation on the origin of the Supper. Calvin puts the clause to a different use, that no authority avails in the Church but the Lord's, since Paul has not contrived a new kind of supper according to his own humour but has Christ as his authority.

The relation to Luke's account then divides two of them. Ellicott observes that Luke agrees most closely with Paul, and infers not that Paul was indebted to Luke, as rationalising critics insinuate, but that Luke valued an account received directly from Christ; and he answers the suggestion that Luke copied this epistle by asking whether the evangelist, had he used it, would have been content with so scanty a record of the resurrection appearances when the ampler account of the five hundred brethren and of James lay at hand. Robertson takes the opposite line without heat, remarking that Luke could easily have read this letter before writing his Gospel.

Ellicott then makes an evidential argument the others do not attempt. In the heated controversies over the Eucharist its evidential value has been lost sight of: if the Betrayal and Crucifixion are not historical, how is the existence of the feast to be accounted for? Here is an epistle whose authenticity the most ruthless criticism has never disputed, witnessing to a rite tied to events twenty years before; and the men who began it were Jews, who spoke of the wine they drank as blood and the bread they ate as flesh. A dark conspiracy might have chosen the tasting of human blood for its symbol, but such a band as the early Christians could not of their own thought have made and published such a choice. Christendom, he ends, was not an afterthought of the Apostles but the forethought of the Lord.

On the words themselves the readings pull apart. Ellicott and Robertson agree that broken is no part of the text, Robertson adding that Luke's given carries the real sense, and that the bread was broken but the body of Jesus was not. Ellicott glosses the command as covering the whole action, to bless, break, distribute and eat, so that these acts make memory grow into realisation of a presence, and wishes the soft music of the words could reach us disentangled from the theological discords of intervening ages; to those who first heard them they implied not a physical presence perpetuated but something to console them for a physical absence. Cyril, from the other end of the tradition, takes them the opposite way: since Christ himself declared of the bread, this is my body, who shall dare doubt, and who shall hesitate to call the cup his blood? Calvin draws a rule of method instead, that in what our Lord did we must consider what he meant us to do, since he did not institute a nightly festival like that of Ceres nor invite men to a spiritual banquet with a full stomach, and actions of Christ not intended for imitation are no part of his institution. Robertson notes that the remembrance meant is ours of him, not his of us. Clarke quotes the canon of Trent anathematising any who deny that Christ here ordained his apostles priests, and answers that whoever believes such an absurdity on such a ground is contemptible. Gill, Henry, Barnes, Wesley and Lightfoot keep to the narrative, Lightfoot noting that its scope and end was commemoration.
25:
The interval between bread and cup is noticed by two. Ellicott says the words after supper are an intimation not found in the first two Gospels, and imply that the blessing of the bread came earlier in the meal. Calvin allows that the Evangelists do not make clear whether the transaction was continuous, and supposes the Lord may have delivered some address between; since he said nothing out of harmony with the sacrament, we need not call the administration interrupted. Ellicott presses the reading covenant rather than testament, noting that new is peculiar to this account and Luke's and does not stand in the best manuscripts of the other two: the cup containing the symbol of the blood is the pledge of a new covenant in blood, set against the old covenant in blood at Sinai. Calvin takes the same word and builds on it, that sacraments are so named because they confirm God's will in our minds, and that if they are covenants they contain promises, so that they are not merely outward signs of profession before men but inwardly helps to faith.

From the two-fold sign Calvin argues the sharpest practical conclusion in the chapter. Christ appointed both, and what God has joined let no man put asunder, so that to distribute the bread without the cup is to mutilate his institution: as he commands us to eat of the one, so he commands us to drink of the other, and to obey one half of a command while neglecting the other is to make sport of it. Keeping the cup from the people, after the priest has drunk of it first, he calls diabolical presumption; and he answers the plea that Christ spoke only to the Apostles as exceedingly childish, refuted from this very passage, since Paul addresses men and women indiscriminately and the whole body of the Church, and says he delivered it by the Lord's own commandment. He closes by asking what wonder it is that men defend in words and writings what they maintain by fire and sword.

What the last verse means by showing is then disputed. Ellicott says the Greek is the word for a public oral proclamation, and denies that the Supper was a living sermon or an acted discourse: what is meant is that an oral declaration was made, perhaps in the very words the Apostle has just used. Robertson takes precisely the rejected view, calling the Lord's Supper the great preacher of the death of Christ till his second coming. Lightfoot supplies a reason why the point needed making: the Passover supper had its own declaration, of the great works of God in the deliverance out of Egypt, and the Judaizing Corinthians appear to have kept that declaration in the Lord's supper, as though the Eucharist were superadded only for it, so that when the apostle insists it is the death of Christ that must be declared, it may be gathered they had erred in this very thing and looked some other way. Clarke sets the two rites side by side without the polemic, that as in the passover they showed forth their bondage and redemption, so in the eucharist they show forth the sacrificial death of Christ. Ellicott restricts as oft as ye drink to this rite, denying that it makes every bodily refreshment a eucharist, and hears in until he come a belief, perhaps largely due to the hope, that the Second Advent was not far off. Calvin says the remembrance meant is one with thanksgiving, whence the rite has its name of Eucharist, though the chief thing is that the efficacy of Christ's death be sealed in our consciences. Wesley, Gill and Barnes keep the plain sense, Wesley adding that the ancient sacrifices were in remembrance of sin while this one is in remembrance of its remission.
27:
The first correction is textual, and Ellicott makes a charge of it. The whole weight of manuscript evidence gives or rather than and, he says, and the conjunction was probably kept in the English version lest the disjunctive should seem to favour receiving in one kind only; but if an interval then separated bread from cup, a partaker might have taken one alone unworthily, and the apostle means that either way he is guilty. Robertson adds a pastoral correction: Paul nowhere implies that we must be worthy to partake, since on those terms none would ever partake, and many pious souls have abstained through false exegesis here. Calvin generalises the case, holding that Paul passes from the fault at Corinth to every kind of faulty administration or reception, with degrees of unworthiness: the openly vicious who intrudes without repentance offers wanton insult, the careless deserves punishment for irreverence.

What the wicked receive draws Calvin's longest argument, entered with reluctance. He notes that some in the heat of controversy say the sacrament is received indiscriminately by good and bad, and that many maintain pertinaciously that at the first Supper Peter received no more than Judas; he would rather not dispute a point he thinks inessential, but others launch thunderbolts at anyone who mutters against them. His own position is that Christ cannot be disjoined from his Spirit, so his body is not received as dead: a man wholly under the influence of Satan cannot receive Christ himself, and those who bring only a historical faith receive nothing but the sign, for he cannot endure to maim Christ.

The self-examination is described in three registers. Robertson makes it metallurgical, a man testing himself as he would a piece of metal to see whether it is genuine, and notes that such scrutiny would have made the earlier scenes impossible. Clarke makes it doctrinal, that a man try whether he has proper faith and whether he discerns the Lord's body. Chrysostom stands back and describes the method: it is Paul's custom to pursue an incidental argument with diligence when it concerns urgent matters, and having found occasion to remind them of the Mysteries he judged it necessary to go on, providing for the sum of all good things, their approaching with a pure conscience.

The last verse divides them twice over. On the penalty, Ellicott says the Greek does not imply final condemnation but only such temporal judgments as the sickness mentioned next, meant to save the man from the final damnation of the heathen; Clarke agrees, the punishment being for the emendation of the disorderly, who are chastened as a father corrects his children. On the body, the readings pull apart. Ellicott, holding the words the Lord's to be no part of the text, argues in four steps that the body meant is the Church: the verb means to arrive at a right estimate; the fault condemned was treating these gatherings as occasions of private indulgence rather than corporate assemblies; referring the words to a physical presence would make the remedy at the end of the chapter no remedy, besides which the blood would surely have been named; and Paul never uses body of Christ's physical body without clear indication. Lightfoot takes it as an act of the understanding, a true judgment of the nature and signification of the sacrament, and identifies the offenders as Judaizers who saw nothing of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, their eyes being too intent on the Passover, so that they kept the old leaven of Judaism in this new one. Clarke reaches the same reconstruction independently, calling them mongrel Christians who used the rite as a historical commemoration and did not discern the body and blood as a sacrificial offering. Robertson keeps to the verb, our discriminate; Gill, Barnes and Wesley take the discerning as putting a right difference between this bread and common food.
30:
Whether the sickness is natural or sent is left open by two and pressed by others. Clarke says it is hard to say whether the words refer to the consequences of their own intemperance or to disorders inflicted immediately by God, observes that continual experience shows many fall victims to intemperance, and quotes the Communion service on provoking God to plague men with divers diseases and sundry kinds of death. Ellicott admits both channels in a phrase, that death sometimes resulted from their drunken orgies either naturally or by God's direct visitation, and corrects the rendering, that many sleep should be some die. Robertson takes the number seriously, observing that Paul evidently had knowledge of specific instances and that a few would be too many. Gill and Barnes read the whole as divine chastisement.

On the judgement itself they converge. Ellicott says the verse explicitly declares that the condemnation following an unworthy partaking was not final but temporal suffering, to save them from being condemned with the heathen; and he notices the change to the first person, courteously identifying himself with them, as characteristic of Paul. Robertson glosses the verb from the word for a child, so that it means to train or discipline, and concludes that afflictions are meant to separate us from the doom of the wicked world. Clarke puts the condition simply, that if having acted improperly we condemn our conduct and humble ourselves we shall not be punished. Wesley and Gill say the same, that the chastening is fatherly and its purpose preventive.

The practical direction is then read two ways. Clarke takes tarry one for another to mean that they should not eat in parties as before, nor connect the Supper with any other meal; Calvin makes it the conclusion of the whole argument, that equality must be observed so that there may be a real participation and no man celebrate his own supper. Lightfoot guards it against a misuse: the apostle is not allowing the ante-suppers of the Judaizers and telling the Gentile part of the church to wait while the Jewish part eats them, for he has already condemned those paschal ante-suppers outright, and means only to take away all dividing into parties so that all may come to the Eucharist together. On the closing promise Calvin allows that other things may have needed better order, or possibly nothing did, since a man knows better when present to see; but he objects that the Papists arm themselves with this buckler too, interpreting the rest as the mass which Paul here promises, as if he would have overturned the appointment of Christ he has just approved, and asks what resemblance the mass bears to that institution, concluding that only outward decorum is meant, which lies in the Church's power to arrange by times, places and persons. Ellicott takes the same phrase as covering further details of the charity-feasts, and notes that when I come carries no indication of an approaching visit but is quite general. He closes with a reconstruction of the rite: the Greeks had a feast to which all contributed and of which all partook, a similar arrangement sprang up among Christians as the charity-feast, and at these gatherings, probably daily at first and afterwards weekly, the Supper was celebrated in two parts, a loaf broken during the meal and a cup taken after it, both marked off by a solemn declaration of the institution which consecrated the whole feast. His last word is an image: communion with Christ and communion with one another intersect and interlace like the threads of a tapestry, indistinguishable while you look at the picture they make, and though theological subtlety may dissever them, to do so is to lose the image on which the early Church gazed with tender adoration and from which it drew the deepest draughts of spiritual life.
